expert.agent_vs_you: The agent trusted the catalogue line 'lettering: true GUARANTEES designed lettering spelled exactly' and put the whole 108-character address in as ONE quoted string, in a single qwen render at 1:1 then a centre crop. It gave no size hierarchy or line plan for the address, and it dropped the user's 'black-and-cream' from the prompt (the planner prompt even uses 'black and cream' as its example of user words to keep). I treat a 108-character address as small print that a 640 px diffusion model will not spell reliably. I would let qwen letter only the three short lines, which it got right in both renders, and set the address with the one tool that guarantees exact characters: text-overlay, by code. The agent could not choose that split. The planner rule says 'One node per designed piece; never a picture node plus a text-overlay for the same design', the WORDS rule sends every flyer word to lettering:true, and nothing in the catalogue says lettering degrades with string length. What sank the output was the harness. Its single fix told qwen to letter the address while also deleting the 'Third address line' and 'Fourth address line' entirely. The fix broke the two lines that had been correct, nothing re-read the result, and the node was marked done with the note 'lettering fixed'.
expert.fix: (1) Harness, the lettering readback in execute.js and buildable.js: a garbled rendering of a WANTED string is a misspelling, never a 'stray' to remove. Fix one quoted line per edit, naming its position. Re-read after every fix, up to 2 rounds, and set the node 'flagged: lettering still wrong' instead of 'done / lettering fixed' when it still misreads. Drop fixText's hard-coded aspect_ratio 16:9 and its 'people, faces, poses, hands' wording for designs. (2) text-overlay: honour extra 'color: #hex; box: none; size: N' (the file header already promises 'box') so long exact text can be set in a design's own colours. (3) Planner rule and catalogue line: exact text over about 40 characters (an address, small print, terms) on a design is lettered by code. The image letters the short headline lines and leaves an empty zone, and text-overlay sets the long text, as a named exception to 'never a picture node plus a text-overlay'.

expert.agent_vs_you: No real divergence. The agent read the request right (one supplied photo, recolour only the hatchback, keep the rest). It picked image-edit with fidelity on, so it ran on qwen, and it said what must stay. The catalogue's own note ('navy came out teal' on klein) is why qwen was the right model. My only change would be the prompt: 'the red car' is ambiguous because there is a second red car parked in the background. I would name 'the red hatchback in the foreground', ask for a deep navy, say the background car stays red, and forbid moving or reframing anything. The failure is in the editor itself. qwen redraws the whole frame and adds a small geometric warp: about a 1.7% horizontal squeeze plus a 3 px shift, with no vertical change. That moves the rear bumper, the plate and the parked cars on the right. The catalogue says plainly that image-edit cannot leave the rest pixel-identical, and no catalogue tool can merge the recoloured body back into the untouched original. The agent could not have reached 'the rest unchanged' with these tools.
expert.fix: Add a 'keep-rest merge-back' to the harness for image-edits where the sheet says keep_rest=yes and the change is local (a recolour, a removal, an added prop). Step 1: register the edit to the original with a global affine fit (block matching finds this one at once: dx runs from +3 px at the left edge to -7 px at the right, dy is 0). Step 2: build a change mask where chroma or luma moved past a threshold (here the car body), then dilate and feather it. Step 3: paste the aligned edit into the original inside the mask only, so every other pixel is the user's own. A code 'recolour' look on the filter tool would also work: hue-map one colour range inside an anchor box, keeping luminance so reflections survive. It is riskier, because the tail lights and the background red car share the hue. Then change the image-edit CANNOT line to 'pixel-identical outside the change (merge-back by code when keep_rest)'.

The swap has to target one face in the API.

Run face detection on the target, choose the face named in extra ("target face: left|right|largest|n"), and send face_mappings for that face only. If a picture has several faces and no target was given, ask which one. Until this is wired, change the catalogue line to "CANNOT: one face among several: it changes every face" so the planner tells the user instead of delivering a double swap.

expert.agent_vs_you: The agent read 'in the first 5 seconds' as an edit range inside the full 10.1 s video. It read 'keep ... everything else' as 'keep the rest of the timeline', so it trimmed the remainder and spliced it back. The deliverable became a 10.1 s video in which the woman's face switches back to the original at 5 s. An expert would weigh three things. First, a face that changes identity halfway through a clip is never a usable result. Second, 'keep the original sound, framing and everything else' lists properties of the frame (the audio, the framing, the kitchen), not the timeline. Third, video face swap costs about 30 credits a second on the free tier, which explains why a user caps it at 5 s. The deliverable is the first 5 s, swapped. The sheet schema pushed the agent wrong: the change branch only has 'range' (default whole) and 'keep_rest' (default yes), with no notion of 'deliver only that range'. So range=0-5 plus keep_rest=yes became a splice. The planner had no rule against an identity switch mid-clip. Steps 1 and 2 were exactly right: opening-swapped.mp4 was 5.0 s, the face was swapped in every sample, and the original audio was intact. Steps 3 and 4 broke the result.
expert.fix: Two changes. (1) Sheet: add a 'deliver' field to the change branch, either 'whole asset' or 'only the range', inferred from the words. 'Swap the face in the first 5 seconds' means only the range. 'Change only the first 5 seconds and leave the rest' means the whole asset. (2) Planner rule: 'An identity change (face swap, lip-sync, dub) on part of a clip delivers that part alone unless the user says the rest of the clip must stay. Never splice a swapped section back into the unswapped original: the face would change mid-clip. keep_rest means keep the picture's other content (sound, framing, background), not the remainder of the timeline.'

I would build the 8 s into the voice track itself: one sentence per line, an unhurried delivery with a pause after each, and the track padded to exactly 8.0 s.

expert.agent_vs_you: The structure of the agent's plan is the one I would choose: one image-to-video of the user's photo, 6 s, 1:1, sound dropped by the harness. The difference is the prompt. The agent wrote 'preserve the bottle's appearance', which only describes the side the model can SEE. A quarter turn forces minimax to invent the side it cannot see, and an unbranded black bottle invites a printed logo there. That is what happened: white garbled vertical lettering and a round badge rotated into view. The agent did not anticipate that rotation reveals unseen surfaces, and nothing in the catalogue warns about it. It also did not say the cap's carry loop is a rigid part, and the loop bent into an open hook mid-turn. I would state that the bottle is plain matte black on EVERY side with no print anywhere, that the cap and loop are one rigid moulded piece turning with the body, and that the camera is locked off on a tripod. That improves the odds, but the deformation and hallucination are minimax-at-480p behaviour that no prompt fully controls.
expert.fix: Add a catalogue line to image-to-video: 'POORLY: turning a product: it paints a logo or text on the side it cannot see and bends thin parts (a loop, a handle, a strap); say the product is plain/unbranded on every side and its parts are rigid, or give an end frame'. Add a planner PROMPTS rule: for any rotation or orbit of a supplied product, describe the hidden side explicitly (same finish, no print) and name the rigid parts. A cheap harness guard: frame at 50% and 100% plus a check ('any text or logo on the product that is not in the source photo?'), retrying once with the negative strengthened when it flags.

expert.agent_vs_you: There is no material to start from, so a single text-to-video shot is correct, at 8 s and 16:9 with sound dropped by code. Where we differ is the prompt. The agent packed the whole action into one clause ('fold the sheet in half, align the edges, then press the crease flat') with no timing, no fold direction and no limit on how many folds. minimax read that as 'some paper folding'. It collapsed the sheet into a narrow, multiply-creased strip in about 0.5 s (0.75–1.25 s), then filled the remaining 7 s with invented origami: diagonal flaps and an envelope shape by 7 s. I would pace the single action across the 8 seconds (fold over 0–4 s, press over 4–8 s), name the fold (bottom edge up to the top edge, one horizontal crease), and say what never happens (no second fold, no flaps, the sheet is never lifted or turned). The agent did not know that a video model compresses a one-line action into the first second and then improvises to fill the time. Even so, hands manipulating paper at 480p remain a hard case for minimax.
expert.fix: Add a planner PROMPTS rule for video: an action with an end state (fold, pour, stack, tie, write) is paced across the clip ('from 0 to 4 s …, from 4 to 8 s …'), says how many times it happens ('folded exactly once') and names what never happens. Otherwise the model finishes the action in the first second and invents more to fill the length. Add a catalogue line to text-to-video: 'POORLY: hands working an object (paper folds, knots, cards): it rushes the action and adds steps; pace it in the prompt'.

It asked assemble for 'smooth cross-dissolves' and 'fit photos without cropping' in extra, but the catalogue line for assemble mentions no transitions and the code ignores both: it concatenates with hard cuts and crops every photo to fill. The agent had no way to know its extra was dropped, and the tool reported success. The fail was then pinned on 'speech' in the soundtrack, which the evidence says is a transcription hallucination on instrumental music, not vocals. So the reel's real defect (hard cuts where the user asked for smooth transitions) is the harness's, and the grader failed it for the wrong reason.
expert.fix: 1) Harness (assemble.js): support transitions: join the parts with xfade (fade/dissolve, 0.4-0.6 s) and lengthen each part by the overlap so the total stays exact; default to dissolves for a photo-only reel and to cuts only when asked; list 'transitions: cut | dissolve' on assemble's catalogue line. 2) Harness: when a step's extra asks for something the tool does not do (dissolves, fit without cropping), report it instead of returning success silently. 3) Grader: do not treat a few transcribed words over a music bed as singing; run a vocal/speech detector or re-transcribe with a 'this may be instrumental music' prompt and require a confident, sustained transcript before calling it speech; also sample frames around the cuts so transitions can be judged.

expert.agent_vs_you: The agent's plan is the catalogue's loop recipe and the one I would draw: a klein still, then image-to-video with that still as both start and end picture, 6 s, 16:9, sound dropped. Its prompts were sensible: fixed camera, only ripples, calm centre, no text. The failure happened after the model returned. minimax-h3 turns a 6 s request into 6.58 s (158 frames at 24 fps), and the harness conforms the aspect and audio but never the length, so a 6.6 s file shipped against an explicit '6-second'. Simply cutting to 6.0 s would also be wrong here: frame 144 (6.0 s) is further from frame 0 (SSIM 0.71) than the model's final frame is (0.86). The right finish is a loop-aware conform that crossfades the extra 0.58 s tail onto the head. That gives exactly 6.0 s with an identical first and last frame. Neither the agent nor the catalogue can express that: trim and assemble would both cut, and the seam would get worse.
expert.fix: Harness, in execute.js after every generated clip: conform the length to params.seconds. When the step's start and end picture are the same file (a loop), take d = duration - seconds and crossfade the clip's last d seconds into its first d seconds (an ffmpeg xfade of [d, L] with [0, d] at offset L-2d). The result is exactly params.seconds, and its last frame equals its first. Otherwise trim the tail, or retime with setpts when within ±10%. minimax-h3 overshoots systematically (4 s → 4.46, 5 → 5.17, 6 → 6.58, 7 → 7.29 across the b2 sessions), so this matters for every single-clip deliverable. Also add a catalogue line under image-to-video: 'a loop is closed and cut to the exact length by code'.

expert.agent_vs_you: The agent planned one crop with "anchor: active speaker; centre the man throughout his question, then centre the woman throughout her answer". That assumes a speaker-tracking reframe the catalogue never offers: crop takes one anchor (left/right/top/bottom/center) for the whole clip. crop.js did not recognise "active" and silently used centre, which frames the dark-shirted bystander in the middle for all 10 s. The questioner is cut at the left edge and the woman is off frame. With the tools listed, the correct plan is to split at the turn: trim the clip at the speaker change, crop each part on its own speaker, then assemble the parts with seconds 0. Assemble keeps clip sound, and seconds 10 would cap each part at 5 s and cut the question. Two gaps made this harder. The agent cannot hear the clip, so it could not know the turn falls at about 7.9 s: there is no transcribe or timing tool. And neither left nor right puts these faces in the middle; the crop tool's undocumented "box: x,y,w,h" does. I measured the turn and the face positions myself.
expert.fix: (1) Add a transcribe tool: clip to text with segment times (gpt-4o-transcribe, 0 Magic Hour credits), so "when he asks / when she answers" becomes trim points. (2) Add to the catalogue for crop: "one static anchor per clip; to follow speakers: trim at each turn, crop each part, assemble with seconds 0"; expose a position ("box: x,y,w,h" or "anchor: 30%"). (3) Make crop fail on an unknown anchor instead of silently centring. (4) Make assemble's seconds a total, not a per-piece cap, so seconds 10 cannot truncate a 7.9 s part.

expert.agent_vs_you: The plan is the one I would make. A code crop to 9:16 with her centred (she is already central, so anchor centre works), then captions on the cropped clip so the subtitles are laid out for the final frame, with the original audio kept. The agent even asked in extra for captions 'below her face'. The miss is in our captions call. execute.js always sends style {template: 'minimalist'}: white text with only a faint shadow. Over her white sweater, 'show you three easy' and 'mornings less stressful' wash out. The API's style.custom_config takes stroke_color/stroke_width, font_style bold and vertical_position, but the harness never passes any of them. It also ignores whatever the planner writes in extra. The catalogue then blames the tool ('styling: big and bold is not honoured'). The agent could not have fixed the contrast with catalogue tools. text-overlay's dark band would need the transcript, which nothing in the catalogue provides. The 'Hi everyone.' versus 'Hi everyone!' punctuation is the transcriber's choice and minor.
expert.fix: In execute.js, send captions a style.custom_config, not a bare template: text_color #FFFFFF, stroke_color #000000, stroke_width about 3-4 px at 480p, font_style bold. Map vertical_position from the planner's extra ('position: top|center|bottom'), defaulting to bottom. Alternatively, pick a template with a stroke or box (test cinematic and highlight once). Then update the catalogue's captions lines to state what is actually controllable: position, an outlined high-contrast style, and no language choice.

expert.agent_vs_you: The agent picked 'video-edit' (Magic Hour's generative ai-video-editor). It was not wired, so the harness wrote a placeholder SVG and reported the step 'done'. Even if wired, it was the wrong tool: a generative editor re-renders footage, and the must-haves demand only source footage with no speed change and the original audio in sync. A cut is a code job, 'trim' (exact range, nothing regenerated), and the catalogue had it. But trim needs a 'from' and 'to', and choosing the 8 interesting seconds needs to SEE the clip. The planner only gets the filename, and no catalogue tool turns a clip into a shot list with timestamps, so the agent had nothing to choose a range from. It probably reached for video-edit because it is the only tool that sounds like it decides what to cut. Looking at the clip: 0–3 s jets cruising, 3–11 s cockpit lines ('Hook, you with me?' / 'Right here, Vega.'), 11.4–16.6 s a static ship with a caption card and a targeting display, 16.6–25.7 s missile launch, hits and the ship exploding, 25.7–29 s jets leaving, then an end card. The best 8 s is the continuous action from the 16.57 s scene cut to 24.57 s.
expert.fix: (1) Add a code 'analyse-clip' inspector (scene cuts via ffmpeg, one described frame per shot, plus a transcript) whose output is a shot list the planner reads. Or run it automatically on every supplied clip and put a short shot list in the MATERIALS line. (2) Planner rule: shortening or 'cutting the boring parts' of the user's footage is trim (one range) or trim + assemble (several ranges), never a generative video editor. (3) The b2 run offered the unwired video-edit, and the executor marks a placeholder 'done'. OFFERED now filters unwired tools, but a placeholder should also make the node 'failed: not wired' so the user hears it.

expert.agent_vs_you: The agent "watched" the clip the only way its catalogue allows: three frames and three vision checks, then a script from what they show ("Two men and a woman smile toward the camera... then turn toward one another"). In a 10 s clip of two coworkers talking, what is happening is what they say (a schedule change; Mondays now start at nine), and frames cannot reveal it. No tool in the catalogue hears a clip. The only stand-in is a detour (captions, about 48 cr, then frame, then check to read the burned subtitles), and the agent did not think of it. It also never noticed that its narration said nothing about the conversation it was replacing. The second failure is in the harness. The agent asked assemble to "remove all original audio", but assemble always keeps a clip's own sound, and because the clip has speech it lays the added voice at 0.25 as if it were music. The original dialogue is still there at full level, louder than the narration. The judge marked that must-have cannot_tell; it is actually a miss.
expert.fix: (1) Add a transcribe tool: clip or sound to .txt with segment times (gpt-4o-transcribe, as the grader already uses), with the catalogue line "WELL: what people in a clip say, with times: a voice-over that explains a conversation, a recut by speaker". Add a planner rule: "explain what's happening / what they say" on a clip with speech means transcribe, then write. (2) Change assemble: accept "clip sound: drop|duck", and treat a voice input as speech on top, not as music under the clip's speech. The tool line already promises "music under speech, not over it". Both changes also serve E25b's speaker timing and any dub or voice-over request.

expert.agent_vs_you: The agent's chain is the catalogue's own recipe for narration (voice, then assemble), with the exact words verbatim and the clip untouched. That is my plan too. Its 'Remove all original audio' instruction went into assemble's extra, which assemble never reads. No catalogue tool can drop a clip's own sound: every video code tool maps 0:a. assemble always mixes the clip's audio in. Worse, it treats any added sound as music: because the clip has audio ('speech'), it puts the narration at volume 0.25 (about -12 dB) under the radio calls, then fades out the last second. So the transcriber heard only 'Rook, you with me?', and 'safely home' was faded away. The voice itself was fine: speech runs from 0 to 6.83 s, followed by 1.36 s of trailing silence, which already meets the 0-0.5 s start and 6.5-7.0 s end windows. The agent's 'target duration 6.8 seconds' was ignored but did not matter here. The only reasoning gap: it trusted free-text extra to change a tool's audio behaviour. The catalogue gave no 'replace sound' option, and an expert would have flagged that before running.
expert.fix: Changes to assemble.js: (1) Support extra 'sound: replace' (or 'clip sound: off'): build the clip pieces with -an or anullsrc so the clip's own audio is dropped. Have the planner set it whenever the sheet says 'replace the sound' or 'remove the original audio'. (2) Do not duck a VOICE input: duck only music (tell the two apart by the producing tool, voice or music). A narration over a clip goes at full level, and the clip's own sound, when kept, goes under it. (3) Fade only music. Trim a voice track's trailing silence instead of fading the last second, so a final word is never faded out. The voice tool should also trim leading and trailing silence and report its speech length against params.seconds. Catalogue: assemble 'extra sound: replace drops the clips' own sound'. expert.agent_vs_you: The finished meme is good: the judge passed all five must-haves, and I agree. The only failure is the question 'What style or mood?' before starting. 'Make a meme about Mondays' is a low-stakes, conventional format. Its style is the meme convention itself (a reaction photo plus bold outlined caption), and an expert would just pick a joke and an image. The question did not come from the planner's judgment but from the sheet's policy. The sheet prompt makes direction 'needed' unless tone, style or message is given or the user says 'your call'. sheet.js then asks the image branch's style field whenever direction=needed and style is unknown. Nothing in that policy recognises formats whose look is implied (meme, sticker, thumbnail, emoji) or a casual one-line request. So the agent asked the question that, as the answer sheet shows, nearly every user answers with 'your call'. After the answer, the plan (write the caption, then one lettered qwen image with the caption fed in as exact words) is exactly what I would run.
expert.fix: In sheet.js, stop asking style or mood by default. Treat it like kind, audience and size: infer it. Ask only when the user's own brand or a high-stakes design is involved and nothing implies a look. At minimum, add to the sheet prompt: 'direction is free (not needed) when the format implies its own look (meme, sticker, emoji, reaction image, thumbnail) or the request is a casual one-liner; style is then inferred with confidence 1.' Harness side note: the lettering fix returned a 16:9 picture that finish() then padded to 1:1 with olive bands. The fix pass should be asked for the step's own aspect.

expert.agent_vs_you: The tree is the right shape: studio stills edited from the user's photo, three 5 s image-to-video shots, a 15 s music bed, assemble, and two code text-overlays. Two of the three faults were written into the agent's own prompts. (1) The closing still asked klein for 'clear space below for a closing caption'. klein, which the catalogue says 'misspells and invents text', painted a caption ('Ridectarp dehaime bultae dliy') that sits under the overlaid 'Shop now' for the last 3 s. (2) Every still and clip prompt said to preserve the bottle's 'existing label' or 'markings', but the bottle is plain matte black with no label. Asking a model to keep a label that isn't there invites one, and the hero push-in grew a large white 'BMOOY' wordmark around 3–4 s. The agent never sees the photo, only its filename, so it assumed a label. I would describe the product as plain on every side, never mention captions or text space in a picture prompt (the overlay adds the words afterwards), and use camera moves rather than product rotation. The third fault, spoken Korean ('여러분 안녕하세요!' = 'Hello everyone!'), can only have come from the music track, because all three shots are silent. The track's spectrogram shows only steady chord stacks and percussive hits, with no speech formants or gliding pitch contours, and that phrase is a classic speech-to-text hallucination on music. So it is most likely a grader artefact (gpt-4o-transcribe on an instrumental bed) rather than real vocals. Nothing in our system can listen to check either way.
expert.fix: (1) Planner PROMPTS rule: never ask a picture or clip model to leave room for, or keep, words ('space for a caption', 'its label') unless they exist. Words added later by overlay are not mentioned to the model, and a supplied product is described as it is ('plain, no label or text'). (2) Feed the planner a one-line vision caption of each supplied picture in MATERIALS ('product-bottle.jpg: plain matte black bottle, no label, on a wooden table'), so it stops assuming labels. (3) Grader: run a voice-activity or music-versus-speech check before trusting a transcript of a music bed. A lone stock phrase on an instrumental track ('여러분 안녕하세요', 'Thank you for watching') should count as a probable hallucination, not 'speech heard'. Harness: the same audio probe as E24c, run on generated music to regenerate genuine vocals. (4) Make each image-to-video's 'no text' explicit by code when the source is plain.

expert.agent_vs_you: Most of the plan is mine too: a generated plain white sneaker, two flux edits for detail and profile views, three 5 s image-to-video shots, one silent assemble at 15 s, then code captions in the safe area. The failure is the last node. The agent put all three captions into one text-overlay, with "caption 1 from: 0; to: 5; caption 2 from: 5; to: 10; caption 3 from: 10; to: 15" in extra. The executor joined every quoted string in the prompt with newlines into ONE card, and text-overlay.js reads only the first "from:"/"to:" pair. So all three captions appear stacked for 0–5 s and nothing appears after that. The agent stretched a format the tool does not parse (in H42a it correctly used one node per caption), but the tool merged them silently instead of honouring the windows or refusing. I would chain three text-overlay nodes, one caption and one window each, all at middle.
expert.fix: Change text-overlay so that when the prompt holds N quoted captions and extra holds N from/to windows (or "caption k from:"), it renders one card per caption for its own window. Today the executor joins all quotes into one card and the tool uses only the first window. Otherwise it should refuse, so the planner chains nodes. Add the planner rule "one text-overlay node per timed caption" and expose a size or max-width so safe-area margins can be met. This covers every timed caption or subtitle sequence.

expert.agent_vs_you: This is the same mistake as D20d. The agent fed the two portrait screenshots (720x1280) straight into assemble and wrote 'fit screenshots without cropping or stretching on a clean neutral background' into extra. assemble never reads that: it always fills the 16:9 frame and centre-crops, which keeps only the middle third of each phone screen. The 'FitTrack' and 'Workout' headers and the first and last rows were lost. The catalogue's CHOOSING line ('Keep ALL of a picture in a new size, crop with fit: contain') covers this exactly, and assemble's guarantee 'the user's photos used as they are' misled it. Second divergence: 'finish with the app name' is an end card. The catalogue routes title and end cards to an image node with lettering true. The agent instead laid a small plain text-overlay band over the last 2 s of the cropped workout screen (the judge's 'weak, cluttered brand finish'). I would contain-fit each screenshot on a plain background in its own header colour, add a lettered 'FitTrack' end card as a third piece, lay a 10 s instrumental beat under it, and let assemble cut the three in order. The 'speech' verdict ('すべての人に') looks like a transcription artefact: the beat's spectrogram shows fixed-pitch synth stabs, not vocal formants. I cannot rule out a vocal chop without listening.
expert.fix: Same fix as D20d, which generalises to every reel or ad built from supplied photos or screenshots. (1) Correct assemble's catalogue guarantee: it crops pictures to fill and pushes in, so a whole picture needs crop fit: contain first. (2) Make assemble honour 'fit: contain' in extra and switch off the 8% push-in on contained pictures; otherwise the top header of a contained portrait screenshot gets shaved by up to 3.7%. (3) Planner guard: a supplied picture whose aspect differs from the target by more than 10% gets a crop fit:contain before assemble unless the user asked for a crop. (4) Planner: 'finish with the name or logo' becomes an end-card image node with lettering true, not a text-overlay. (5) Grader: confirm a speech claim on a music bed with a vocal-presence check before failing.

expert.agent_vs_you: The agent knew klein misspells, so it tried to dodge text: a demo screen 'with checkbox icons and abstract blue lines instead of written words', on klein with lettering off. That failed twice. klein still painted a garbled header ('DyVmning') and section labels ('Dsure Ensues'), as the catalogue warns it 'invents text'. And a to-do app whose tasks are blue strokes is not a credible demo, which is the judge's major fault. An app screen is a designed piece whose words carry the meaning, so I would make both demo states on qwen with lettering on and short real task names, quoted so the readback checks them. Because the catalogue says image-to-video 'CANNOT: readable text inside the motion', I would not morph lettered cards. I would show the change as a before/after inside one assemble: messy state, organised state (an image-edit of the messy one on qwen, so the style matches), then a designed ClearDay end card. The cut shows the transformation with every word exact. The agent also asked text-overlay for 'navy text on a white band'. The tool cannot do that (white text on a fixed translucent dark box), so it produced the dark-grey slab the judge called disconnected; a lettered end card avoids it.
expert.fix: (1) Planner rule: a UI, app screen, dashboard, menu or chart mock-up is DESIGNED LETTERING. It goes on qwen with lettering true and short real words, never klein with 'no words' (klein invents them anyway). (2) Catalogue line under image-to-video: 'a before/after of a lettered screen is two lettered pictures cut together in assemble, not a morph'. (3) text-overlay: honour the colour and band asked for in extra (color, box: none, band colour), or reject the instruction so the planner knows. Today 'navy text on a white band' silently became white on dark grey.

Catalogue: add to assemble's line that "pictures get a slow push-in (gentle movement, 0 credits)", so 'gentle movement' of photos does not send the planner to image-to-video. expert.agent_vs_you: The agent sent an 8-second, one-person, one-shot talking-head ad to the six-stage film chain. Its reason was 'because the presenter speaks on camera'. It was obeying a misleading planner rule: film is never for an ad or a clip of 20 s or less, 'unless the user names ... characters on screen speaking their lines (then film wins, whatever the kind)'. The same prompt's catalogue has the direct path: 'A face that speaks → talking-photo', with voice for the exact words. An expert sees one fictional presenter, one fixed selfie framing, 14 exact words and 8 s. That is a still of the presenter, a synthetic voice reading the script verbatim, a talking-photo to make her speak, and exact captions laid on by code. The film chain also hands exact captions and timing to a pipeline the planner does not control. The bench records film plans without running them, so nothing was made and the item scored 0. Even when run, the film chain is built for stories over 20 s.
expert.fix: Rewrite the planner rule in plan.js. Today it reads '... or characters on screen speaking their lines (then film wins, whatever the kind)'. Make it: 'one presenter or one talking head speaking to camera in a single setting, 30 s or less (testimonial, UGC ad, announcement, greeting) is a tree: image (or the user's photo), then voice (the exact words), then talking-photo, then captions or text-overlay. Film is only for several characters or several scenes.' Add a price-aware guard: a film plan whose total is under 20 s with one character is re-planned as a tree. Catalogue: talking-photo WELL 'a presenter or testimonial to camera'. Harness side note: the bench pass records film plans unrun, so a wrong film choice costs the whole item.

expert.agent_vs_you: The agent's design work was right and the cards came out perfect: a qwen '3' poster, then qwen edits of it for '2', '1' and the event card, all lettered exactly and consistent in style. It wrote the timing it wanted in assemble's extra: 'countdown_3 0–1 s; countdown_2 1–2 s; countdown_1 2–3 s; event_end_card 3–8 s'. assemble.js ignores that and gives 4 pictures 8/4 = 2 s each, so the cuts landed at 2, 4 and 6 s and the end card had only 2 s against the required 3 or more. Same defect as D23a and E29b. With today's tools I would build each piece at its own length first: three 1-second card clips and one 5-second end-card clip, each a one-picture assemble. Then I would join them with seconds 0 (own lengths) and extra 'music: full'. The flag is needed because the silent tracks on those clips would otherwise make assemble duck the music to 25% as if there were speech. The 'speech' fault is doubtful. The judge only reads a gpt-4o-transcribe transcript, which returned one Sinhala word ('පෙම්වතුන්') for an electronic bed whose spectrogram shows synth harmonics, a riser and a pitch-bend, which is typical ASR hallucination material. I also would not name 'countdown' or 'voices' in the music prompt, since negations can prime vocal samples.
expert.fix: (1) Same assemble.js fix as D23a and E29b: per-piece durations from extra ('durations: 1,1,1,5' or the planner's 'X 0–1 s' wording). Also, a clip's silent track must not count as speech when deciding to duck music: check its loudness, not just whether an audio stream exists. (2) Optional harness sync: detect the music's main energy jump (the drop) and move the reveal cut onto it, so 'accents matching the numeral changes' is by construction. (3) Grader: gate transcripts of music beds with voice-activity detection. A single word in an unexpected language over an instrumental track is a probable hallucination.

expert.agent_vs_you: The agent built one 16:9 master and centre-cropped it to 9:16, betting on its still prompt ('musicians grouped in the central third'). A 9:16 crop of 16:9 keeps only 32% of the width; the model spread four or five musicians across the whole frame and the push-in widened them further, so the vertical version cuts the right-hand guitarist through the face at ~1-4 s. The user asked for both versions to 'fill the frame', which rules out padding, so the only safe route for a group of people is a native composition per aspect: recompose the wide still as a vertical one (an image-edit keeps the same musicians and look) and animate each. That costs a second clip, the price of not cutting faces. The text and audio parts of the agent's plan were fine. The judge's other fault ('speech' in the portrait audio) is a transcription artefact: the 16:9 version carries the same music track and was not flagged.
expert.fix: 1) Planner rule / CHOOSING line: 'Several aspect versions of footage with people (a band, a group, two speakers): make each aspect natively (image, then an image-edit recomposing it into the other aspect, then image-to-video for each); never centre-crop 16:9 to 9:16, which keeps a third of the width. Crop only when there is one centred subject.' 2) Catalogue crop POORLY: 'groups spread across a wide frame: a 9:16 crop of 16:9 cuts the people at the sides'. 3) After any crop of footage with people, run frame + check 'is any face cut by the frame edge?'. 4) Grader: the transcription guard (the same track was 'speech' in one version and clean in the other).

expert.agent_vs_you: The agent resolved 'the ending' correctly to seconds 5-8 and kept the opening by trimming it, which is right. For the new landing it then planned 'video-edit', a tool the catalogue never offered: catalogue.js filters it out of OFFERED because it is unwired. Make the landing picture by an image-edit of the original's last frame, with the plane now resting on an open blank notebook. Animate from the cut frame to that end frame (image-to-video with start and end pictures, which the catalogue lists as WELL: 'a move from one picture to another'). Then assemble the untouched opening and the new 3 s clip. The harness made the failure silent. The unwired tool ran as a placeholder SVG and was marked done, and assemble quietly dropped the SVG and delivered 5 s, so a 5-second video came out as 'done'. One more trap the agent avoided only by luck: assemble with seconds 8 and two clips gives each an equal 4 s share, which would cut the opening to 4 s. My plan sets seconds 0 so both clips keep their own length.
expert.fix: Harness: (1) Refuse a plan step whose tool is not in OFFERED before running anything. Re-plan, telling the planner the tool does not exist, instead of writing a placeholder SVG and marking the step done. (2) Make assemble fail when a declared input is missing or not a picture or clip, instead of silently dropping it and delivering a shorter video. (3) Make assemble's seconds allocation give clips their own length and spread only the remainder over pictures (today share = T/n cuts a 5 s clip to 4 s). Do not add an anullsrc track when no piece has sound. Planner rule: 'Change part of a clip = trim the part to keep, frame at the cut, image-edit the new end state, image-to-video from the cut frame to that end frame, then assemble.' Catalogue: 'no tool edits a clip's content in place'.

expert.agent_vs_you: Turn 1: for a 'cosy illustrated look' the agent went straight to text-to-video, following the catalogue's 'A free scene → text-to-video'. Its style word was a vague 'illustrated', and minimax rendered a glossy, near-photoreal cup with reflections. Only the floral curtain at the left edge read as illustration. The catalogue already warns that illustration drifts to photographic on the image model, and video drifts at least as much. The reliable path is to pin the style in a still and animate it: an image whose prompt LEADS with a concrete style (flat 2D storybook gouache, ink outlines), then image-to-video, which keeps its start picture's look. Turn 2: told 'make it for TikTok instead … same idea and length. Go ahead and make it now', the agent applied the reframe rule and centre-cropped the 16:9 clip. That kept the photoreal look, cut away the one illustrated element (the curtain), and upscaled a 270x480 strip to 720x1280. A platform change on a piece the user never approved is a fresh make at native 9:16, not a crop. The clip existed only because the bench runner executes every plan with steps, including turn 1, which the user had asked to see as a plan only.
expert.fix: (1) CHOOSE rule: 'MOTION: a named visual style (illustration, watercolour, anime, claymation, storybook) → image first with the style leading, then image-to-video; text-to-video drifts to photoreal'. Extend plan.js guard()'s STYLE prefix to text-to-video and image-to-video prompts, not just image prompts. (2) Planner rule: 'same idea, new platform or size' for a clip the user has not accepted means regenerate at the native aspect; crop only when the user wants the existing clip reframed. (3) Bench runner: honour a plan-only turn ('just tell me your plan') by not executing it, as the app would wait for approval. Otherwise the follow-up turn is graded on a state the user never asked for.
